title: Kenya Airways 431
summary: Kenya Airways Flight 431 crashed into the Atlantic Ocean shortly after takeoff from Abidjan on 30 January 2000 at night. The crew responded to a false stall warning by pushing the control column forward, placing the aircraft into an unintended descent. The GPWS warnings were masked by priority stall and overspeed warnings in conditions with no external visual references. The Commission of Inquiry concluded the pilot applied stall recovery procedure while the airplane was not in a true stall situation.
probable_cause: The crash was caused by the pilot flying applying one part of the procedure, by pushing forward on the control column to stop the stick shaker, following the initiation of a stall warning on rotation, while the airplane was not in a true stall situation. The pilot flying's action on the control column put the airplane into a descent without the crew realizing it. The GPWS warnings were masked by priority stall and overspeed warnings. The conditions for takeoff towards the sea at night provided no external visual references.

factors.evidence: Just seconds after takeoff, at the moment when the first officer requested the landing gear to be retracted, the stall warning sounded in the cockpit.
The pilot flying told the captain to silence the stall warning and put the aircraft into a controlled descent.
The GPWS warnings could have alerted the crew to an imminent contact with the sea were masked by the priority stall and overspeed warnings
the conditions for a takeoff performed towards the sea and at night provided no external visual references
The aircraft crashed into the Atlantic Ocean
The airframe was completely destroyed by the impact.

events.text: Just seconds after takeoff, at the moment when the first officer requested the landing gear to be retracted, the stall warning sounded in the cockpit.
The first officer told the captain to silence the stall warning and the aircraft was put into a controlled descent.
The GPWS sounded briefly, though the radio altimeter sent out warnings seconds after, cutting off the GPWS warning.
The master warning sounded, indicating that the aircraft was overspeeding.
The aircraft crashed into the Atlantic Ocean, 2 km east of the airport, off the Ivory Coast.

title: Air Philippines 541
summary: Flight 541 approached Davao City behind a Philippine Airlines Airbus A320. When the crew observed the preceding aircraft had not cleared the runway, they advised ATC and initiated a missed approach. Instead of climbing to 4,000 ft on instruments and circling as procedure requires, the pilots attempted visual flight at low altitude in instrument conditions. The aircraft struck a coconut tree 500 ft above sea level.
probable_cause: The pilots attempted to fly under visual flight rules in instrument meteorological conditions at a lower than required altitude, resulting in controlled flight into terrain.

factors.evidence: skies were foggy at the time of the accident
pilots did not fly correct missed approach procedure but instead attempted VFR in instrument conditions
aircraft climbed and re-entered clouds but pilots continued at low altitude instead of proper missed approach
pilots attempted to maintain visual references in instrument conditions
Flight 541 hit a coconut tree about 500 ft above sea level and crashed

title: Air France 4590
summary: Air France Flight 4590 ran over debris on the runway dropped by a preceding Continental Airlines DC-10, causing a tyre to explode and disintegrate during takeoff at 185 mph. Tyre fragments struck the underside of the Concorde wing, damaging the landing gear and rupturing the integral fuel tank. Large amounts of fuel leaked and ignited, causing loss of thrust in engines 1 and 2. The aircraft lifted off but the loss of thrust, high drag from extended landing gear, and fire damage to flight controls made it impossible to maintain control. The Concorde crashed into a hotel in Gonesse two minutes after takeoff.
probable_cause: A titanium alloy wear strip dropped by the preceding DC-10 caused the Concorde tyre to explode, tyre fragments ruptured the fuel tank, and the ensuing fire disabled engines and flight controls.

factors.evidence: Continental Airlines Flight 55 DC-10 lost a titanium alloy wear strip about 435 mm long that was part of the engine cowl
tyre fragment impact sent out a pressure shockwave that ruptured the number 5 fuel tank at its weakest point just ahead of the left landing gear well
Leaking fuel gushing out from the bottom of the wing was ignited either by an electric arc in the landing gear bay or contact with hot parts of the engine
Engines 1 and 2 both surged and lost all power due to ingestion of hot gases and tyre debris
aircraft had passed V1 speed but did not gain enough airspeed with three remaining engines as damage to landing gear bay prevented retraction of undercarriage
aircraft crashed into a hotel in nearby Gonesse two minutes after takeoff, killing all 109 on board and 4 on ground

events.text: Continental Airlines Flight 55 DC-10 departed from runway 26R and lost a titanium alloy wear strip about 435 mm long from the engine cowl
Concorde ran over the piece of debris at 185 mph during its take-off run, cutting the right-front tyre of the left main wheel bogie
Large chunk of tyre debris struck the underside of the left wing, sending pressure shockwave that ruptured the number 5 fuel tank
Leaking fuel was ignited and large plume of flame developed; Engines 1 and 2 both surged and lost all power
Air traffic controller noticed flames and informed flight crew that aircraft was on fire, but aircraft had passed V1 speed at which takeoff is unsafe to abort
Concorde crashed into a hotel in Gonesse two minutes after takeoff, killing 109 people on board and 4 people in the hotel

title: Singapore Airlines 006
summary: During heavy rain from Typhoon Xangsane with poor visibility, the aircraft was cleared for takeoff but lined up on the closed runway 05R instead of the assigned runway 05L. The pilots did not see construction equipment on the closed runway and collided with excavators and other machinery after 41 seconds at full throttle. The aircraft broke apart and caught fire, destroying the forward fuselage section. The accident exposed systemic failures including the lack of ground radar, absence of physical barriers or hazard markings on the closed runway, and active taxiway lighting that guided pilots into the construction zone.
probable_cause: The flight crew lined up on the wrong runway due to poor visibility and turned 215 meters too soon. However, the investigation found that ATC cleared takeoff without operational ground radar and the airport lacked proper physical barriers and hazard markings on the closed runway.

factors.evidence: Visibility was poor in the heavy rain caused by Typhoon Xangsane; the aircraft left the gate during heavy rain
The aircraft left Bay B5 of the airport during heavy rain caused by Typhoon Xangsane
The crew attempted takeoff on runway 05R, which had been closed for repairs, instead of the assigned runway 05L
The captain correctly acknowledged that he needed to take off on 05L, but he turned the aircraft 215 m too soon and lined up on 05R
The airport was not at the time equipped with ASDE, which is a ground radar that enables air traffic controllers to detect potential runway conflicts
The runway contained concrete Jersey barriers and pits, but there were no physical barriers or hazard markings on the closed runway
About 41 seconds after applying full throttle, the aircraft collided with construction machinery including excavators, vibrating rollers, a bulldozer, and an air compressor parked on runway 05R
A large fire destroyed the forward section of the fuselage and the wings

events.text: The aircraft left Bay B5 of the airport during heavy rain caused by Typhoon Xangsane
Ground control cleared the aircraft to taxi to runway 05L via taxiways SS, WC, and NP
The aircraft was cleared for takeoff in heavy weather during Typhoon Xangsane.
The crew attempted takeoff on runway 05R, which had been closed for repairs, instead of the assigned runway 05L; the captain turned the aircraft 215 m too soon
After 41 seconds at full throttle, the aircraft collided with construction equipment including excavators, vibrating rollers, a bulldozer, and an air compressor on the runway
The aircraft broke into three major pieces; the fuselage was torn in two, engines and landing gear separated, left wing torn off, and nose struck a scoop loader causing a large fire

title: 2000 ASA Pesada Antonov An-24 crash
summary: On 15 November 2000, an Antonov An-24 operated by ASA Pesada crashed shortly after taking off from Quatro de Fevereiro Airport in Luanda, Angola, banking left before hitting a field in the Golfe II district and exploding; all 57 aboard were killed. A preliminary investigation found the crash was caused by engine failure and also cited ASA Pesada for negligence in failing to keep accurate records of the fuel quantity and passenger numbers on board.
probable_cause: A preliminary investigation found the accident was caused by engine failure, and also accused operator ASA Pesada of negligence for failing to keep accurate records of the amount of fuel and number of passengers on board.

factors.evidence: the accident was caused by engine failure
the report also accused ASA Pesada of negligence for failing to keep accurate records of the amount of fuel and number of passengers on board
eyewitnesses stated that during the crash, the Antonov An-24 was on fire
the aircraft then banked to the left and crashed onto a field in Golfe II district of Luanda

events.text: A preliminary investigation found the accident was caused by engine failure shortly after takeoff.
The aircraft banked to the left and crashed onto a field in the Golfe II district of Luanda.
Eyewitnesses said the Antonov An-24 was on fire during the crash.
The aircraft exploded on impact, and authorities evacuated 40 badly burned bodies from the crash site.

notes: cause is from a preliminary investigation only, not a final report
